claims.text: The transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition is driven by a percolating network of coherent, compositionally modulated SRO clusters in the B2 phase.
The SRO clusters are potent, non-dissociable obstacles to dislocation glide.
Dissolution of the SRO network at higher temperatures restores ductility.
The initial alloy has a lamellar or rod-like microstructure comprising a ductile FCC matrix and a hard, ordered B2 phase.
The initial alloy contains no significant grain-boundary segregation.
Aging at 400–600°C permits atomic diffusion while avoiding grain coarsening and phase decomposition.
Intermediate-temperature aging nucleates SRO clusters without providing enough thermal energy to dissolve them or induce phase separation.
L1_2- or D0_3-type SRO precursors form within the B2 phase and at FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
The SRO network increases the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation entry into the B2 phase.
Solute ordering in the B2 phase creates a high density of coherent SRO clusters during intermediate-temperature aging.
The coherent SRO clusters generate significant local lattice-strain fields.
The SRO clusters increase the energy barrier for dislocation cross-slip and entry into the B2 phase.
Dislocations cannot cut through the ordered domains without high applied stress.
Restricted dislocation motion in and near the ordered domains leads to brittle fracture.
At higher temperatures, thermal energy overcomes the ordering energy and dissolves the SRO clusters.
The ductility minimum should coincide with a maximum in yield strength.
The ductility minimum should coincide with a peak in SRO-cluster density measured by diffuse scattering.
Ductility should recover when the SRO clusters dissolve at higher aging temperatures.
The proposed embrittlement regime excludes grain-growth-dominated temperatures above 1000°C.
The proposed embrittlement regime excludes impurity-segregation-dominated temperatures below 300°C.
